title: The DAO recursive-split reentrancy attack path
mechanism: The DAO's splitDAO function transferred ETH to a child DAO before zeroing the caller's balance, and the caller's fallback could re-enter splitDAO with the still-credited balance, recursing to drain the parent DAO.
root_cause: Checks-effects-interactions violated: external transfer before the state (balances) was updated, enabling unbounded recursion.
preconditions: attacker holds a positive DAO balance
splitDAO performs the ETH transfer before setting balance to 0
the receiving address can re-enter splitDAO via fallback (a contract, not EOA)
call_sequence: splitDAO transfers ETH to attacker child DAO
attacker fallback re-enters splitDAO with the same balance
each recursion transfers the credited amount again
recurse until the DAO is drained
attacker_permissions: any DAO member with a positive balance
tx_conditions: attacker address must be a contract with a re-entrant fallback
cross_function_deps: splitDAO depends on balances[] also mutated by newDAO/withdraw
impact: ~3.6M ETH diverted from the DAO in 2016.
remediation: See source postmortem for the fix; the pattern is: eliminate the state/write ordering flaw (CEI), harden the oracle source (TWAP/depth/manipulation resistance), or enforce a timelock/guard so the compromised prerequisite cannot be reached in one tx.

title: bZx margin-trade oracle manipulation via flash loan
mechanism: Attacker flash-loaned ETH, used it to manipulate the Kyber/Uniswap price of sETH (a thin liquidity pair), then opened a margin trade on bZx whose collateralization was priced off the manipulated oracle, extracting real ETH at the inflated price.
root_cause: bZx priced a large margin trade off a spot oracle (Kyber) that routed through a thin Uni pool the attacker could move with the flash-loaned capital; no manipulation-resistance or depth check.
preconditions: bZx allows opening a margin trade against a spot-price oracle
the oracle price is derived from a thin liquidity pool (low depth)
attacker can flash-borrow enough ETH to move the pool price
call_sequence: flash-borrow 10k ETH from dYdX
swap on Uni/compound to push sETH price
call bZx.borrow with sETH as collateral (priced high)
bZx sells sETH collateral for ETH
repay flash loan, keep the extracted ETH
internal_calls: bZx.borrow -> oraclize price fetch -> collateral calc
state_deps: pool reserves write -> oracle price read (bZx) -> collateral read (bZx)
attacker_permissions: none (anyone can open a flash loan / margin trade)
tx_conditions: sufficient flash-loan capital to move a thin pool
cross_function_deps: borrow depends on the price snapshot computed before collateral is posted
remediation: See source postmortem for the fix; the pattern is: eliminate the state/write ordering flaw (CEI), harden the oracle source (TWAP/depth/manipulation resistance), or enforce a timelock/guard so the compromised prerequisite cannot be reached in one tx.

source: Curve Vyper read-only reentrancy (2023) — public postmortem
title: Curve Vyper pools read-only reentrancy (cross-contract)
mechanism: A Vyper compiler bug let an attacker re-enter a Curve pool's remove_liquidity via a malicious ERC-20 callback while the pool's balances were mid-mutation; a second contract (the consumer) read the pool's unstable virtual price/balances and acted on the corrupted state, letting the attacker drain the consumer.
root_cause: Vyper 0.2.15/0.2.16 omitted the reentrancy guard on certain view paths; the pool's state was inconsistent during the callback and the consumer's read used it.
preconditions: pool compiled with vulnerable Vyper versions
a consumer contract reads pool balances/virtual price during the callback window
attacker controls an ERC-20 token used by the pool (CRV/frax-amount callback)
call_sequence: attacker enters remove_liquidity
pool transfers a token -> malicious token contract fallback fires
attacker re-enters pool (view state inconsistent) or calls consumer
consumer (e.g. lending/balancer) uses the corrupt virtual price/balances
exit and profit
state_deps: token transfer (external) precedes balances update -> view reads are unstable
tx_conditions: attacker deploys a malicious token contract
consumer must read the pool during the callback
cross_function_deps: remove_liquidity state write is deferred past an external call; views read it
impact: ~$61M drained across multiple Vyper Curve pools (July 2023).
remediation: See source postmortem for the fix; the pattern is: eliminate the state/write ordering flaw (CEI), harden the oracle source (TWAP/depth/manipulation resistance), or enforce a timelock/guard so the compromised prerequisite cannot be reached in one tx.

source: Beanstalk governance flash-loan attack (2022) — public postmortem
title: Beanstalk flash-loan governance takeover
mechanism: Attacker flash-borrowed 1B BEAN, used it to pass a governance proposal (emergency governance, no timelock) that transferred protocol funds to the attacker, repaid the flash loan, and kept the loot — all in one transaction.
root_cause: Governance execution had no timelock between passing and executing, and voting power was flash-loanable (on-chain balance snapshot with no borrow-resistance).
preconditions: emergency governance allows immediate execution after quorum
voting power is computed from a flash-loanable balance
the proposal can move funds (transfer function exposed to governance)
attack_entry: executeProposal / vote() with flash-loaned voting power
call_sequence: flash-borrow 1B BEAN
vote YES on a malicious proposal (quorum reached)
execute the proposal immediately
proposal transfers ~$180M of protocol funds to attacker
repay the flash loan
keep the stolen assets
state_deps: balance read (voting power) -> proposal status write -> treasury transfer
attacker_permissions: any token holder with flash-borrowed voting power
cross_function_deps: vote -> execute are separate functions with no delay between them
remediation: See source postmortem for the fix; the pattern is: eliminate the state/write ordering flaw (CEI), harden the oracle source (TWAP/depth/manipulation resistance), or enforce a timelock/guard so the compromised prerequisite cannot be reached in one tx.

title: Wormhole signature verification bypass
mechanism: The Solana-side Wormhole contract's initialize() could be called by anyone (no ownership check after deployment), letting the attacker set the guardian set and sign a forged 'observed' message that minted 120k wETH on Ethereum.
root_cause: initialize() lacked an ownership/initializer guard, so the guardian-set upgrade path was callable by an attacker who could then forge signed messages.
preconditions: initialize() is externally callable without an owner check
postMessage/verify signature logic trusts the guardian set set in initialize
attacker can call initialize() before/without authorization
call_sequence: call initialize() with attacker's guardian set
craft a forged 'observed' cross-chain message (mint 120k wETH)
verify() passes because the attacker controls the guardian set
mint wETH on the target chain
internal_calls: verify -> guardian set read -> signature check
external_calls: (cross-chain) Ethereum mint call via forged message
state_deps: guardian set write (initialize) -> signature verify read -> mint
tx_conditions: must call initialize() before the legitimate owner
cross_function_deps: verify trusts the guardian set written by initialize
remediation: See source postmortem for the fix; the pattern is: eliminate the state/write ordering flaw (CEI), harden the oracle source (TWAP/depth/manipulation resistance), or enforce a timelock/guard so the compromised prerequisite cannot be reached in one tx.

source: Parity multi-sig wallet bug (2017) — public postmortem
title: Parity library selfdestruct bricking 150k ETH
mechanism: The Parity WalletLibrary's initWallet function could be called on the library itself, and one attacker's call to kill() (after becoming library owner via initWallet) self-destructed the shared library, making every dependent wallet unable to execute any code path (all funds frozen).
root_cause: The shared library exposed its own initialization and kill functions to arbitrary callers; the library address itself was callable directly, so anyone could initWallet on the library and then kill it.
preconditions: library is callable directly (not just via delegatecall from wallets)
initWallet has no guard preventing use on the library itself
kill/selfdestruct is reachable by the library owner
call_sequence: attacker calls initWallet on the library address itself
becomes owner of the library
calls kill() on the library
library self-destructs
all 587 wallets become unusable (funds frozen)
cross_function_deps: initWallet grants ownership that kill consumes
cross_contract_deps: all wallets delegatecall into the shared library
remediation: See source postmortem for the fix; the pattern is: eliminate the state/write ordering flaw (CEI), harden the oracle source (TWAP/depth/manipulation resistance), or enforce a timelock/guard so the compromised prerequisite cannot be reached in one tx.

source: Nomad bridge root-update attack (2022) — public postmortem
title: Nomad bridge uninitialized-proxy message forgery
mechanism: Nomad's Replica was deployed as an upgradable proxy whose initialize() was never called, so the trusted root was the zero hash. Anyone could call process() with a message whose root matched the zero hash (or copy another attacker's valid message), bridging arbitrary funds out.
root_cause: The proxy was left uninitialized (trusted root = bytes32(0)), and process() accepted messages against that root; a valid spoofed message drained the bridge, then copycat transactions followed.
preconditions: Replica proxy deployed without calling initialize()
process() accepts messages whose root equals the current (zero) trusted root
attacker can construct a message + proof that hashes to the accepted root
call_sequence: attacker calls process() with a forged message
proof/root check passes against the zero trusted root
bridge credits the message (mint/release funds)
copycat attackers replay the same pattern after the first drain
state_deps: root read (zero) -> message accept -> funds transfer
tx_conditions: message must hash to the accepted (zero) root
cross_function_deps: process trusts the root that initialize() was supposed to set
remediation: See source postmortem for the fix; the pattern is: eliminate the state/write ordering flaw (CEI), harden the oracle source (TWAP/depth/manipulation resistance), or enforce a timelock/guard so the compromised prerequisite cannot be reached in one tx.

source: Mango Markets oracle manipulation (2022) — public postmortem
title: Mango oracle price manipulation via large collateral deposit
mechanism: Attacker deposited a huge amount of MNGO (their own token) as collateral on Mango, which raised the MNGO/USD price through the on-chain oracle, then borrowed the entire borrowable USDC against the inflated collateral and let the position default.
root_cause: The oracle allowed a single user's large collateral deposit to move the asset's price (no manipulation resistance, no depth weighting), and borrow limits scaled with the inflated collateral.
preconditions: oracle price is derived from the deposit/spot ratio on the protocol itself
borrow limit is a function of collateral value at that price
attacker owns a large supply of the collateral token
call_sequence: attacker deposits ~1B MNGO as collateral
oracle MNGO price rises with the deposit
attacker borrows ~$116M USDC against the inflated collateral
position becomes underwater; protocol socializes the loss
external_calls: (none required; oracle is on-chain perp price)
state_deps: collateral write -> price write -> borrow limit read
cross_function_deps: deposit's collateral inflates the price that borrow uses
remediation: See source postmortem for the fix; the pattern is: eliminate the state/write ordering flaw (CEI), harden the oracle source (TWAP/depth/manipulation resistance), or enforce a timelock/guard so the compromised prerequisite cannot be reached in one tx.

source: Ronin bridge validator compromise (2022) — public postmortem
title: Ronin bridge validator-set compromise
mechanism: Attacker socially engineered Axie/Sky Mavis validator keys, reached a 5-of-9 signature threshold (4 Sky Mavis validators + 1 Axie DAO validator), and signed 2 forged withdrawals transferring 173k ETH + 25.5M USDC out of the Ronin bridge.
root_cause: The bridge trusted a fixed multi-sig validator set whose private keys were centrally held; compromise of enough keys (5 of 9) authorized forged withdrawals with no additional verification.
preconditions: withdrawal requires 5-of-9 validator signatures
validator private keys are centrally/insecurely stored
attacker can compromise 4 Sky Mavis + 1 Axie DAO key
call_sequence: compromise 5 validator keys
sign 2 forged withdrawal messages (173k ETH, 25.5M USDC)
submit to the Ronin bridge
bridge releases the funds to attacker addresses
state_deps: validator set read -> signature check -> funds release
cross_function_deps: withdraw relies on the validator set managed by governance
cross_contract_deps: Ronin bridge <- validator keys (off-chain) -> Ethereum withdrawals
remediation: See source postmortem for the fix; the pattern is: eliminate the state/write ordering flaw (CEI), harden the oracle source (TWAP/depth/manipulation resistance), or enforce a timelock/guard so the compromised prerequisite cannot be reached in one tx.

source: Cream Finance AMP flash-loan attack (2021) — public postmortem
title: Cream AMP token price manipulation via flash loan
mechanism: Attacker flash-loaned AMP, dumped it on the AMP/USDC Uniswap pair to crash the price used by Cream's oracle (which took AMP/ETH from Uni without manipulation protection), then deposited the cheap AMP as collateral at the crashed price, borrowed ~$130M in other assets, and repaid the flash loan — the collateral was overvalued by the manipulated price.
root_cause: Cream's oracle used a Uniswap spot price for AMP that a flash-loaned dump could crash; collateral was priced at the manipulated value.
preconditions: oracle reads spot Uni price with no TWAP/depth protection
AMP has a thin Uni pair (low liquidity)
flash loan capital is large relative to pair liquidity
call_sequence: flash-borrow AMP
dump AMP on Uni AMP/USDC (price crash)
deposit AMP as collateral (at the crashed oracle price)
borrow ~$130M against the overvalued collateral
repay flash loan, keep borrowed assets
internal_calls: deposit -> oracle price read -> collateral value
state_deps: pool price write -> oracle read -> collateral value write -> borrow read
cross_function_deps: deposit's collateralization reads the price the swap just crashed
remediation: See source postmortem for the fix; the pattern is: eliminate the state/write ordering flaw (CEI), harden the oracle source (TWAP/depth/manipulation resistance), or enforce a timelock/guard so the compromised prerequisite cannot be reached in one tx.
